title: Robinhood Markets: The Distribution Moat Meets Its Supplier
subtitle: Kalshi's push into equities turns Robinhood's fastest-growing trading partner into its newest rival.
summary: Robinhood built an empire by collecting tolls on retail trading, but its fastest-growing product runs on pipes owned by an exchange that now wants its equity customers. The stock's next leg depends less on a crypto comeback and more on whether it can reclaim the plumbing.

bodyHtml:
Pull your phone from your pocket, and Robinhood sits right there between your banking app and food delivery. It is a commission-free brokerage built for 29 million funded customers who prefer fast trades on clean glass. The platform does not charge an upfront commission at the register. Instead, it runs a toll booth on retail risk appetite. It sells order flow to market makers, earns interest on a $22 billion margin book, collects subscription cash from 5.2 million Gold members, and clips fees on crypto and event contracts.

That setup turned Robinhood into a powerhouse by cornering the retail crowd. Its real competitive moat was never proprietary technology; it was raw distribution. Millions of high-turnover traders kept that green feather on their home screens. But distribution moats crack when your key supplier decides to bypass the middleman. Robinhood is learning what happens when you rent the storefront instead of owning the real estate.

The sudden threat comes from prediction markets. On November 16, reports surfaced that Kalshi, the event-contract exchange powering Robinhood's buzziest bets, bought a New York broker-dealer named FB Securities. Kalshi plans to roll out direct stock and ETF trading within months. Kalshi raised fresh funding at a reported $40 billion valuation and held talks at $65 billion, rivaling Robinhood's roughly $62 billion equity size. Robinhood helped make Kalshi a household name. Now, that supplier wants Robinhood's stock-trading customers.

This is not just another retail turf battle. It strikes directly at Robinhood's fastest-growing revenue line. Third-quarter crypto transaction revenue plunged 55% year over year to $120 million. Stepping into that vacuum were event contracts, exploding sixfold to $173 million. Trading political and economic outcomes now generates more revenue than crypto. Yet Robinhood operates that surging product desk on rented rails.

The fee mechanics explain why this matters. Every event contract carries a two-cent fee, typically split between broker and exchange. On the estimated 60% of volume that routes to Kalshi, Robinhood collects only one cent. When flow heads to Rothera, its joint venture with Susquehanna, Robinhood keeps both cents. That structural split explains why Robinhood's calculated revenue per contract slipped from 1.18 cents early this year to 1.05 cents last quarter.

For the equity to re-rate higher, Robinhood does not need a crypto renaissance. The real multiple expansion depends on whether the company can bring that prediction volume in-house. Migrating that estimated 60% Kalshi flow to Rothera would mechanically inject nearly $98 million in quarterly revenue on flat volume. Management wants the vast majority of volume on Rothera by early 2027. If revenue per contract climbs back above 1.5 cents while quarterly volume holds above 5 billion contracts, the equity narrative changes from tenant to landlord.

The short case argues that Robinhood is handing distribution to a competitor while its own core growth engine stalls. Net revenue growth decelerated from 32% in the second quarter to 12% in the third. Operating expenses rose 16% over the same period, creating negative operating leverage and causing net income to drop 14%. The forward multiple near 20 times forward earnings sits well below the three-year average near 36 times tracked by Goldman Sachs, but that cheaper multiple reflects slower growth. The bears will be proven right if fourth-quarter revenue growth slides below 5%, event-contract revenue drops below $173 million, or Kalshi launches equities with tighter pricing.

Leadership is brushing off the challenge. Mizuho reported that management does not view Kalshi's entry as a strategic threat, citing ten years of customer retention and product refinement. The core engine still brought in $80 billion of net deposits over the trailing twelve months, pushing platform assets past $380 billion.

The non-trading legs are compounding too. A Gold credit card sits at 1.3 million holders with $19 billion of annualized payment volume, still without general availability. Retirement assets are up 51%, and roughly 200,000 AI-agent trading accounts have opened. But regulatory friction is mounting alongside competitive heat. Nine Democratic senators recently urged the CFTC to halt decisions that override state-level prediction market bans, directly targeting Robinhood's highest-volume sports territory.

What we are watching next sits in the mid-December operating report. That release will show whether November crypto volume stabilized and whether Rothera is capturing a bigger slice of prediction flow. Robinhood proved it could gather the retail crowd. It now has to prove it can keep them when the supplier opens a competing storefront downstairs.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in HOOD. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
